title: Serbia's national heat-price methodology undermined by flat-rate billing and local approval
programme: Decree on the Methodology for Determining the End-consumers Price of Heat Supply (2015)
problem: Serbia's 58 municipally owned district heating companies need tariffs that recover their costs, but heat supply is a communal service priced under local control.
solution: A government methodology sets cost-plus tariffs with the rate of return capped at 10%, which companies calculate and local authorities approve; if a local authority sets a lower tariff it must compensate the company for the difference.
implementer: Government of Serbia and municipal and city governments
funding: Heat tariffs paid by consumers, with municipal compensation where the approved tariff is below the calculated one.
results: Only 15 of 59 district heating companies had implemented consumption-based billing, and the source finds that across the region tariffs are rarely adjusted to fuel costs in practice.
serbia_reason: This is Serbia's own district heating tariff regime. Limited metering and local control over prices leave companies short of the revenue needed to modernise.
adapt_needed: Assign tariff control to one independent authority, as the source recommends for Serbia, and roll out heat meters so consumption-based tariffs can apply.
blockers: Municipalities own the companies, take 50% of their profit and face political pressure to keep heat prices low.
quote: Tariffs based on consumption should apply as a principle, while a normative tariff based on heated area can apply if consumption-based billing is not technically possible. Only 15 of 59 district heating companies implemented consumption-based billing.

title: Kosovo's energy regulator sets heat tariffs but fuel spikes still need bailouts
programme: Law on Thermal Energy and ERO Rulebook for determining heat prices (2016)
problem: Kosovo's four municipally owned district heating companies are natural monopolies whose tariffs need independent control.
solution: The national Energy Regulatory Office itself calculates cost-plus heat tariffs each year, with two-part tariffs, metered or area-based billing, accounting unbundling and an end-of-period correction for over- or under-recovery.
funding: Heat tariffs; in one case, central government subsidies for fuel oil (mazut).
results: The source rates Kosovo's tariff transparency as good, but when the fuel price rose sharply the central government had to subsidise fuel purchases because one company could not finance fuel through its tariffs.
serbia_reason: Kosovo shows the national-regulator model that the source recommends for fragmented, municipally approved heat tariffs such as Serbia's.
adapt_needed: Serbia would need to give its energy regulator heat-tariff powers and a fast rule for passing fuel-cost changes through to tariffs.
blockers: Municipalities would lose control over heat prices, which they use to protect households.
quote: In practice, there was a case when the central government had to intervene with subsidies allocated for the purchase of fuel (mazut) for heat production, since the fuel price increased significantly and the company could not finance the fuel by itself through tariffs.

title: Lithuania's competitive heat wholesale market cut average heat prices 35%
programme: Law on Heat Sector reforms: competitive wholesale heat market
problem: District heating companies are natural monopolies, so without competition or oversight heat prices can stay above efficient costs.
solution: Since 2010 Lithuania has opened the heat wholesale market so independent producers can inject renewable heat, while the regulator VERT sets base prices for 3-5 years and fuel and purchased-heat costs pass through monthly.
results: The average heat price has fallen by 35% since 2012, and biofuels now supply around 60% of district heat.
serbia_reason: Serbia's gas-dependent district heating could lower costs by letting independent renewable heat producers sell into municipal networks.
adapt_needed: Serbia would need rules and charges for third-party access to heat networks, which its methodology lacks, plus accounting unbundling.
blockers: Serbian heat companies are vertically integrated municipal enterprises with little incentive to buy heat from competitors.
quote: Namely, the wholesale market became competitive, enabling third parties to inject heat produced from renewable sources. As of 2012, the average heat price in Lithuania decreased by 35%.

title: Denmark's municipal heat planning and non-profit tariffs drive renewable district heating
programme: Heat Supply Act: non-profit heat tariffs and municipal heat planning
problem: Heat networks are natural monopolies where prices can climb; some privately owned Danish companies raised heat prices by more than 50%.
solution: Tariffs may include only necessary costs, with a profit specifically allowed for renewable, heat pump and surplus-heat producers; municipalities plan heat supply, and new or renovated systems must first prove they are the least-cost option.
implementer: Danish municipalities and the Danish Utility Regulator (Forsyningstilsynet)
funding: Heat tariffs, plus low-interest loans for district heating companies through a credit system.
results: Over 400 district heating companies supply heat to 64% of Danish households, and about 58% of district heat came from renewable sources in 2016.
serbia_reason: Serbia's municipalities already own their heat companies and could adopt least-cost heat planning before modernising or expanding networks.
adapt_needed: Serbia would need municipal heat-planning capacity and a low-interest credit line for heat companies.
blockers: Serbian heat companies must pay 50% of their profit to their municipal owners, leaving little for reinvestment.
quote: A pre-condition for construction or renovation of a district heating system is a pre-feasibility study showing that the system is the least cost option compared to alternative sources.

title: Bosnia's locally set heat tariffs lack clear cost rules and oversight
programme: Local tariff systems for district heating in Sarajevo and Banja Luka
problem: With no state-level district heating law, each canton, city or municipality in BiH sets its own heat tariff rules.
solution: Local governments in Sarajevo and Banja Luka adopt tariff methodologies based on production costs and planned maintenance, approve company-calculated tariffs and cover the gap when tariffs are set below cost.
implementer: Government of Canton Sarajevo and City of Banja Luka
funding: Heat tariffs, with local budgets covering the gap when prices are set below actual costs.
results: The local methodologies do not define eligible costs, the regulatory asset base or depreciation, tariff changes are published only once they take effect, and the Competition Council found abuse of dominant position in some tariff proposals.
serbia_reason: Serbia also leaves heat tariff approval to municipalities, so BiH shows the risks of local control without clear cost rules or independent oversight.
adapt_needed: Serbia would need clear national cost definitions and an independent third party to resolve tariff disputes, as the source recommends.
blockers: Local governments' dual role as owners and price-setters creates conflicts of interest.
quote: In practice, the Competition Council issued several opinions on the proposals of tariff systems of district heating companies, in some of them finding abuse of dominant position.
